Working With the Subconscious Mind: How Many Pieces to Work With?

Working With the Subconscious Mind: How Many Pieces to Work With? In my posts, the words “subconscious”, “unconscious”, “feeling body”, “subpersonalities” etc. are meant to point to the part of your mind that is responsible for perception, emotion, desire, avoidance, imagery, memory, bodily signals, habit patterns, intuition, and automatic behaviour. Sometimes it’s helpful to work with this part of your mind as a whole, and sometimes it’s more helpful to work with it in a precise and differentiated way.

Working With Subpersonalities vs. Working with Higher Self It’s helpful to move back and forth between working with subpersonalities for precision and working with Higher Self for coherence. Here are some examples:
Working with Higher Self for Coherence “Oh, wise subconscious mind, what would you show me?”

Working with Subpersonalities for Precision “There are parts of my subconscious that want love like a child, parts that want to keep me safe, parts that want to criticize, parts that want to create fantasies, parts that hold the body’s memories, parts that want social acceptance, parts that want connection to God or source or to the benefit of all, and wiser parts that want what is really best. How do I work with all of these parts?”
Starting with Higher Self When You’re Fragmented “Oh, Higher Self/ universal heart-mind/ wise subconscious mind, what would you show me?”

Differentiating Subpersonalities When Needed “Which part is afraid? Which part wants to protect me? Which part wants to avoid this? Which part has the answer I’m looking for? Which part is too young for this?”
Integrating Again into One “My whole mind wants to live one life together, led by the love of the adult self.”
Sometimes, Start With the Whole If you’re too fragmented to even start working with parts, it’s better to start by seeing your whole being as sacred:

“I’m going to approach this from the perspective of universal heart or Higher Self, or from the part of me that existed before I took on all these roles and families and groups and stories and ideas and ideologies and identities and situations in my life.”

If you can’t approach it from the point of view of Higher Self or universal heart yet, then you can start by being the Witness of your experience, noticing your room and your body and that you were younger at some point in your life.

If you can do that, you don’t really need to work on being the Witness any more, and you can go straight to developing whatever inner function you need, such as inner warmth, or inner protection, or inner direction. Working with Higher Self is a good way to do this, because it helps you gather your resources around something meaningful. Just believing that you have inner parents is not going to make them appear – you have to develop them!
Differentiating Subpersonalities When Needed “Is this inner child or protector or body or fear or intuition or social programming or divine guidance?”
Start from Heart, Differentiate When Needed, Return to Heart Again

old: Sometimes the inner-child question lands nowhere because a private self had very little room to develop. In controlling families, rigid religions, enmeshed communities, or high-pressure achievement systems, performance can begin so early that a person doesn’t know what they feel, want, believe, or prefer until somebody else tells them first. Then “love yourself” produces a reasonable question: love whom? Reparenting and identity-building can proceed together. For some people the child-self is already easy to feel. For others, creating enough safety for preference, curiosity, and experimentation is part of how that self becomes easier to hear.
This may apply when:
You do not know what you want unless someone else says what they want first.
Your opinions shift dramatically depending on who is in the room.
You agree in the moment and later realize you did not agree.
You feel responsible for other people’s emotions to the point of self-erasure.
Self-love feels performative.
The question “What does my inner child feel?” produces guesses, not felt answers.
You can rebel, but you cannot yet choose.

A useful developmental explanation is that when childhood is organized around avoiding pain and preserving attachment, attention goes into reading danger, meeting expectations, and keeping the bond. That can leave less room for the ordinary experiments that answer, “What do I like? What do I want to try? Who am I when nobody is grading me?” This is a practical model, not a claim about one specific brain system.

Sometimes a temporary, intentional period of distance from the people or group supplying the answers helps quieter preferences surface. Use that distance only long enough to tell your own signal from the social echo; prolonged isolation would undermine the purpose.

The difference between a human doer and a human being helps here. When worth isn’t felt internally, it gets earned through beauty, performance, intellect, status, spirituality, or becoming indispensable to everybody else. Those can all be real gifts. They become belonging bargains when failure in the arena feels like losing yourself.
Useful questions:

“What do I like when no one is watching?” “What do I believe before I check whether others approve?” “What do I want that is neither rebellion nor compliance?” “Where am I buying belonging with self-betrayal?” “Which arena am I using to earn the right to belong?” “What would I try if nobody needed to be impressed?” “Which relationships let me remain myself?” “What am I noticing in my body, and what meaning am I giving it?”

Give the inner child a small experiment with no résumé value: painting, dancing, gardening, a language, a sport, volunteering, music, or anything else you’re allowed to be bad at. The inherited parent may demand immediate talent. The adult can answer, “We’re finding out whether we enjoy this, not proving our worth.” Give it enough repetitions to get past the humiliation of being a beginner.

For a child, belonging can feel like survival, so families, religions, romances, political tribes, spiritual groups, institutions, and online communities can reach astonishingly far into identity. Adulting means noticing where you buy belonging with self-betrayal, choosing your own ground, and learning that you can disappoint someone without disappearing. The subconscious contains a crowd of borrowed voices, which is why this belongs in a self-hypnosis guide.
“Where do I become less true in order to remain included?”
“What would belonging look like if I did not have to disappear?”

“Is this guidance, or is this a belonging program?” “Is this love, or is this fear of exclusion?” “Is this conscience, or is this conditioning?” “Is this devotion, or is this compliance?” “Is this rebellion, or is this freedom?”
Then wait for the body. It isn’t infallible, but it deserves a seat at the hearing.
new: Working with your inner child can be harder when you did not have a private self to begin with. This happens a lot when people come from a background where their family, religion or community took over their life very early on, or they were pressured to achieve in a certain way at a young age. This means that you don’t know who you are, what you feel, what you want, what you believe, what you like, or what you don’t like until you hear what someone else says first. This makes it hard to follow the advice to “love yourself” when you don’t know who “yourself” is. So in these cases, reparenting needs to go hand in hand with finding yourself. For some, it’s easy to work with their child-self because they can feel their child-self really easily. For others, it requires creating safety and playing around more to feel their child-self.
You might be in this camp if:
You don’t know what you want until you hear what someone else wants
You find that your opinions change dramatically depending on who is around
You catch yourself agreeing with someone when you didn’t agree in the moment
You tend to take responsibility for other people’s emotions to the detriment of yourself
Trying to love yourself feels like a performance
Trying to find out how your inner child feels, results in guesses instead of feeling
You find that you can rebel, but you can’t choose

The reason for this is that a part of your brain didn’t have the opportunity to explore “what do I like?” and “what do I want to try out?” because as a child you were focused on finding ways not to hurt yourself or lose attachment.

Sometimes it is necessary to distance yourself for a certain period from the people or group that you are getting your answers from so that you can distinguish between what you want and what you are told to want. However, you don’t need to do this for long – just long enough to differentiate what is yours from what is social.

This means moving from a “human doer” to a “human being”. If you don’t feel like you are good enough just because you exist, you will try to create a sense of worth by being beautiful, by doing something well, by being smart, by gaining status, by being more spiritual than everyone else, or by being needed. In all of these cases, you are essentially making a bargain with yourself – that as long as you are good at something (or good at being good for other people), you will be good enough to belong. And if you fall short in that arena, you feel that you are not good enough.
To help you find yourself, ask yourself these questions:
What do I like when no one is watching?
What do I believe before I check what other people think?
What do I want that is not in rebellion to others, and is not in compliance with others?
Where am I buying my sense of belonging by betraying myself?
What “arena” am I using to try to buy my sense of belonging?
What can I try on for size that I don’t need to impress anyone with?
What relationships allow me to be myself?
What do I notice in my body and what meaning am I attaching to it?

Remember that your inner child needs to play! Try out some things that have no value towards your resume – painting, dancing, gardening, learning a language, a sport, volunteering, playing music, etc. Your parent may be telling you that you are supposed to be good at something as soon as you start doing it. Your job as your own parent is to remind yourself that you are not doing these things to prove your worth – you are doing them to see if you like them or not. And it will take some time before the humiliation of being a beginner goes away.

As a child, belonging was essential to your survival. As an adult, it can manifest in families, religions, romantic relationships, political tribes, spiritual groups, institutions, or even online. Part of “adulting” is finding out where you are trading your sense of self in exchange for belonging, and then consciously choosing where you want to belong – on your terms. A large part of your subconscious mind is made up of the voices of other people, so this is also a good opportunity to use some of the tools in this self-hypnosis guide to help you let go of them.
Where am I betraying myself in exchange for belonging?
What would it feel like to belong without having to betray myself?
Is this my own guidance or a belonging program I adopted?
Is this love, or is it a fear of being excluded?
Is this my conscience or is it conditioning?
Is this devotion, or is it compliance?
Is this rebellion, or is it freedom?
Then see what your body tells you.

old: Self-hypnosis also teaches influence literacy: noticing when somebody else is already shaping your attention. Screens, advertising, politics, religious fear, erotic imprinting, charismatic authority, belonging pressure, shame, urgency, and repetition all do it. Influence is everywhere—a lullaby, a prayer, a good teacher, a beautiful song, love. Ask what it does to your ability to see and choose.
new: One of the best side-effects of learning self-hypnosis is an increased awareness of all the ways you’re being manipulated in your day-to-day life. By a screen? By a specific ad? By a politician? By a religion? By erotic imprinting? By an authority figure? By the desire for belonging? By shame? By a sense of urgency? By repetition? It’s all around you. Sometimes it’s benign – like lullabies or prayers or being taught by a good teacher or listening to a beautiful song or being in love. But you may want to ask yourself what effect it’s having on your ability to see clearly and make choices.

old: Pause there. Don’t obey immediately, and don’t perform automatic rebellion either. Wake up inside the influence.
new: If you’re being hypnotically influenced, stop. Don’t listen. Don’t rebel, either, just stop and realize that you’re being influenced.

old: Hypnotic language turns manipulative when it smuggles in your consent, makes one choice seem inevitable, or hides a disputed claim inside the sentence.
new: Some common ways hypnotic language becomes manipulative includes:

old: “When you finally admit…” “As you realize I’m right…” “The only reason you resist is…” “Part of you already knows…” “Your higher self wants…” “Everyone who is truly awake understands…” “If you doubt this, that proves your ego is afraid.”
new: “you’ll realize, eventually, that…” “you may eventually admit that…” “the reason you’re not feeling it yet is…” “even if part of you doesn’t feel that’s true…” “your higher self knows…” “everyone knows…” “the reason you don’t believe that’s true is your ego’s fear of…”

old: The grammar assumes the conclusion, turns resistance into proof, and makes obedience feel like awakening.
new: Other language patterns to watch out for include:

old: “What exactly is being claimed?” “What choice is being framed as inevitable?” “What is being presupposed?” “Who benefits if I accept this frame?” “What emotion is being amplified?” “What information is missing?” “Can I say no without being punished, shamed, mocked, abandoned, or spiritually downgraded?”
new: Is it telling you what you’re going to do or experience? Is there an implied lack of choice? Is it presupposing things that may not be true? Who benefits from you being in this frame of mind? Is it ramping up emotions that aren’t serving you? Is it not giving you information you should have? Can you easily say “no” without there being consequences (shame, getting mocked, not being let into the group, being labeled “unspiritual,” etc.)?

old: A useful guide leaves the adult self more present. Powerful states need stronger boundaries.
new: Even a good guide should be helping you to bring your adult self into the experience more. The more powerful the state, the more you should have boundaries.

old: Permissive words can still conceal coercion. I watch for the following:
new: Language that’s permissive but that still takes your choice away includes:

old: Indirect suggestion can slip past the skeptical guard because the conscious mind may never receive one clean proposition to accept or reject. The intended direction can still be quite specific even when the wording feels open, vague, conversational, or merely suggestive.
new: Utilizing indirect patterns, which often work better because they bypass the conscious mind, but can be specific about where they’re going even if vague in their language, may just seem conversational, or use suggestions.

old: Induction hidden inside explanation: attention is being narrowed while the speaker pretends only to inform. Even an “anti-hypnosis” lesson can use induction mechanics.
new: Using induction patterns while seeming to “explain” things (even some of my explanations of how to avoid hypnosis use some of the mechanics of induction).

old: Every answer means compliance: “yes,” “no,” noticing, not noticing, resistance, and silence are all redefined as proof that the suggestion is working.
new: Setting it up so that any response the listener gives is compliance (answering “yes” or “no,” noticing something, not noticing something, resisting, not responding).

old: “Whether you notice it or not” binds: uncertainty is converted into invisible success that cannot be checked.
new: Using bind patterns (“whether or not you notice…”).

old: Identity and ownership language: safety or goodness becomes tied to obedience, a role, the guide’s approval, or belonging to someone else.
new: Telling you who you are or using language that makes you feel like you “belong” to the guide or that being “good” or “safe” comes from obeying the guide or a role.

old: Unannounced fractionation: moving in and out of absorption without telling you that repeated re-entry is part of the method.
new: Fractionating you without telling you they’re doing it.

old: Hidden post-session cues: words, gestures, blinks, sounds, or repeated listening are meant to produce later behavior that was not plainly disclosed.
new: Using post-session cues (gestures, blinks, sounds, even having you listen to something more than once) that they haven’t told you about that will make you do something later.

old: Amnesia or truth inflation: dreamlike material, missing memory, imagery, or body sensations are treated as proof of what happened.
new: Making you forget things, telling you something is true, utilizing “dream logic,” utilizing imagery or body sensations to make you believe something is true.

old: An exit that does not exit: the recording ends while preserving a role, reduced judgment, impaired movement, blankness, or an indefinite altered state.
new: Not actually letting you “out” at the end of the recording, leaving you in a role, or leaving you in a state where your ability to use good judgment or move your body is impaired or leaving you blank or in an altered state for an indefinite amount of time.

old: A real choice includes at least one branch that doesn’t continue the induction: make it lighter, change the method, remain fully alert, pause, or stop. No remains no. Silence and uncertainty don’t become consent because the narrator has a soothing voice.
new: Make sure you have a real choice to not proceed with the induction at any time, make it more gentle, use a different way, not be in an altered state at all, or stop or pause the induction and know that “no” really means “no.” Even not responding or not being sure should not be taken for “yes” just because someone’s voice sounds nice.

old: Appendix C has the longer de-hypnosis checklist.
new: For a longer de-hypnosis checklist, see Appendix C.

old: Reverse whatever you used to enter. If you floated, regain chosen weight. If you became small, return to ordinary scale. If you met a younger state or several parts, confirm present wholeness, body ownership, and adult judgment. If you traveled, come back by the same route. Keep only the qualities you deliberately chose.
new: Come out of the session by reversing the entry method; if you floated, come back down by the same method; land with your chosen weight. If you shrunk, come back to your normal size. If you meet your younger self or parts, make sure that you acknowledge that you are now whole, this is your body, and you are using your adult judgement. If you traveled, then come back the same way you left. Make sure that you are only bringing back what you had intended to bring back.

old: “I bring back only what is useful now. The rest can remain safely held until there is more capacity. I return to the room, the body, the day, and one honest action. All instructions to deepen or remain in this session are finished. I keep only the ordinary-life intention or future-practice cue I consciously chose; neither keeps today’s altered state running. I am myself, in my body, with adult judgment fully available.”
new: You may wish to say, “I am bringing back only that which I choose to bring back at this time. All that is not needed at this time will remain safely stored away until such time as I am ready. I am now coming back to this place and to my body and to normal day to day living. All instructions given to me in this session are now over except for the conscious intention (or cue) to implement in the future.”

old: One — feel the body’s contact and chosen weight. Two — let the breath return to its ordinary rhythm. Three — hear the room and name where you are. Four — move fingers, toes, shoulders, and eyes. Five — eyes open, present, ordinary, clear. The session has ended.
new: Count yourself out: 1. Coming back into your body and your chosen weight. 2. Coming back to your normal breathing pattern. 3. Coming back to awareness of your surroundings and of your location. 4. Moving your fingers and your toes and your shoulders and your eyes. 5. Opening your eyes, feeling present, normal and clear. Your session is now over.

old: Name the day or date. Look left, right, near, and far. Move before standing, and stand only when steady. Check that you are actually oriented and alert; repeating the count is not proof of a complete return. Note only what actually appeared, and any action it calls for. Then do something normal.
new: It is a good idea to say to yourself what day it is or what the date is, look to your left and to your right, look at something near and something far away, move about a bit before you stand up, stand up and make sure that you are oriented and alert. Take note of anything that came up during your session and what you may or may not need to do as a result, and then just go about doing something normal.

old: If a recording stops unexpectedly: say, “The recording stopped and the session is over.” Open your eyes, name the location and day, press your feet or hands into a surface, move, look around, and use the five-step count. Don’t wait for the missing narrator to release you.
new: In the event that a recording that you are listening to stops unexpectedly, simply say to yourself “the recording has stopped and the session is over” and then use the above method to come out by opening your eyes, saying where you are, saying what day it is, pushing down with your feet or your hands, moving about, looking around and then using the 5 step method.

old: Sleep is separate. A sleep recording may end in sleep or quiet rest. A waking recording shouldn’t end by preserving a role, reduced judgment, impaired movement, blankness, an undefined reset word, or an invitation to remain altered indefinitely.
new: Note: If you are using a recording to go to sleep, then it is all right to let the recording put you to sleep or have you in a quiet resting state. However, if you are waking when the recording ends, then it should not leave you in any state that is not conducive to normal functioning, such as leaving you in a role, with lowered judgement, impaired movement capabilities, blank or with an undefined reset word, etc.

old: Sit rather than lie down when you tend to daydream, dissociate, or fall asleep. Let the spine rise without becoming military, soften the jaw, and keep some awareness of the room. Save lying down for sleep, deep rest, or dream incubation.
“I am not leaving life. I am listening more deeply to life.”
Begin by invoking the larger field:

“Higher Self, universal heart-mind, wise subconscious, body intelligence, inner child, inner adults, protective parts, and all that serves truth and love: please help me understand what I need to know, only in the form and timing that is useful, kind, stabilizing, and real.”
You’re asking the conscious mind to listen without forcing an answer.

Thoughts do not have to stop before deeper listening begins. Let thoughts, sensations, images, doubts, and emotions pass through awareness without fighting or following them; keep the intention lightly in the background and notice what becomes salient on its own.
“Please tell me what I need to know, or ask what you need to know. I will wait silently for five minutes.”
The response may be a phrase, sensation, memory, color, child, protector, pain, warmth, silence, task, gratitude, an urge to stop, or the realization that today’s practice is over.
Listen to all of it. Believe none of it automatically.
new: Make sure you are not lying down when you do this exercise, unless you are ready to go to sleep or receive deep rest or are trying to incubate dreams. Sit in a place where you will not find yourself daydreaming, dissociating or going to sleep. Keep your spine straight, but not rigid, like a soldier. Relax your jaw and maintain some connection with the room you are in.
You can say to yourself, “I’m not going to leave life, I’m just going to listen more deeply to life.”

Invoking: “With the help of my Higher Self, my universal heart-mind connection, my wise subconscious mind, the intelligence in my body, my inner child, my inner adults, my protective parts and everyone and everything else that can help me to know what I need to know, only what I need to know in a useful, kind, stabilizing, real way…
Ask your conscious mind to listen.

This doesn’t mean you have to silence your thoughts to listen. Notice your thoughts, sensations, images, doubts, emotions, etc., without fighting them, without going with them, but simply noticing them while you hold the intention of this exercise in the background of your mind. Notice what becomes salient to you.
You can say, “Tell me what I need to know or tell me what I need to know to ask, and I will sit in silence for five minutes and listen.”

You might hear a phrase, feel a sensation, notice a memory, see a color, be contacted by a child or protector, feel pain, warmth, silence or know that your need to do something or be grateful for something or that this is enough listening for today.
Listen to it all and believe none of it.

old: Use the same practice rather than learning a second script: gather attention, listen, respond, wait, return. Fifteen minutes is a convenient appointment with yourself, not a therapeutic dose or a timetable your feelings must follow. Use a few minutes to enter, leave several minutes to return, and let the middle unfold at its own pace. Five minutes of silent listening is available when useful; you can interrupt it to change direction.
new: You may choose to do all of this practice, or learn the second script. Either way, you'll be using a similar process and can use these recordings as a base for your own practice. These exercises only need to be done for fifteen minutes or so. This is not a therapeutic time, but merely enough time to induce yourself (a few minutes), do what you are going to do (in this case 5 minutes of sitting in silence and listening), and then bring yourself back out again (a few minutes). You can break out of the process at any time, if you feel you need to do something else.

old: Another simple entry is to notice three things you see, three you hear, and three bodily sensations; then two of each, then one. Count from five to one and begin listening. Use the entry that suits you, rather than stacking inductions.
new: B) Notice three things you can see, then three things you can hear and three sensations you can feel in your body. Now do two of each, then one of each. Count from 5 to 1 and start listening.

old: After familiar runs, shorten a recording to the cues you still need, then try practicing without playback. Keep recordings when you enjoy them; independence means being able to guide yourself, not having to refuse help. The optional re-entry cue can shorten an already familiar induction.
new: After practicing a few times with these scripts, feel free to edit them down and remove any parts that you feel are no longer necessary to help you induce yourself. The idea is that eventually, you will not even need to play them back. But there is no harm in using them if you enjoy it. (Note: in script A, the part about coming back out again is optional; if you are familiar with the induction process, it will probably be enough to simply count).

old: Afterward, ask what needed warmth, what needed protection, and what direction serves truth, love, and life. Was there something to explore, or capacity to build? What can you carry yourself now? When action is needed, make it concrete: “If [cue] happens, then I will [small action].” Check how you sleep, relate, and function later, not only how impressive the session felt.
new: When you come out of the process, consider whether there is anything you would like to nurture with more warmth, or protect, or direct in a way that moves it in the direction of truth and love and life. Perhaps there is something you would like to explore or build up. You may want to take this process with you as you move about your day. If there is something you need to do, then make a plan with yourself to do that thing. Be concrete and say something like, "If _________ , then I will do________ ." Then see how things are later on: how you are sleeping, relating and functioning.

old: Once or twice a week, give the same practice more time when that is useful. More time needn’t mean greater intensity. Start from Higher Self or neutral witnessing, follow what appears, borrow an adult function when needed, and ask whether anything important is being bypassed. Leave room for the full exit and any ordinary action needed afterward.
new: Practise this once or twice a week and spend a bit more time with it if that would be useful but don’t make the practice any stronger. Whenever it is useful just access Higher Self, or if that is not possible go to a neutral witnessing place and let it unfold, using any adult function that is necessary to recognise any bypassing that may be going on and always allowing for a full exit and any necessary normal action.

old: Do the ordinary action immediately when possible. That teaches the subconscious that the adult heard and acted, instead of staging another beautiful internal meeting and then leaving the dishes exactly where they were.
new: Wherever possible take any normal action immediately afterwards to impress on the subconscious that something has changed, otherwise it may think that because the dishes have not been done, despite all the internal meetings to do the dishes, that there is no point in doing them.

old: Altered-state rule: do not ask for hidden truth while medically unsafe, panicking, sleep-deprived, nauseated, destabilized, manic, psychosis-like, or chemically overwhelmed. First stabilize. Truth that requires destabilization is not ready to be known directly. Ask for capacity, not content.

Sometimes it feels as though the subconscious knows something the conscious mind can’t yet tolerate. The subject may be sexuality, grief, trauma, family truth, betrayal, shame, vocation, relationship reality, illness fears, spiritual calling, addiction, identity, or moral conflict.
Interrogation is the dangerous response:
“Tell me now.” “Reveal everything.” “Stop hiding.” “I demand the truth.”

That pressure can produce flooding, panic, false certainty, confabulation, dissociation, or a generally worse Tuesday. Flooding can make the adult capacities needed for pausing, comparing options, reality-testing, planning, and choosing much harder to reach. In that state, regulation and support come before deeper dialogue. Silence may be protection when the adult lacks enough regulation, support, humility, or practical capacity to receive the material.
Ask for the next tolerable piece:
“Do I need to know the content now, or do I need to build capacity first?”
“What would make the conscious mind 5% more able to receive this?”
“Can you show me the truth as a symbol, not a full revelation?”
“Can you give me the next protective action without revealing the whole story?”
“Who, if anyone, should help me hold this?”
A safer script:

“Wise subconscious, if there is something I cannot yet handle, please do not break it open violently. Help me become someone who can know it safely. Give me preparation before revelation. Give me grounding before memory. Give me support before intensity. Give me one next action.”

Hypnotic imagery can be meaningful without being literal. The mind symbolizes, compresses, distorts, dramatizes, and borrows from culture and fear. Around trauma and memory especially, treat an image as an image and involve outside support when needed.
new: NOTE: If it is medically unsafe for you to do this, or you are panicking, sleep deprived, nauseated, deeply destabilized, manic, in a psychosis-like state, or overwhelmed by chemicals, please stabilize first before seeking out what your subconscious needs you to know. It is not ready for you to know it if it requires you to destabilize to know it!

There are times when your subconscious seems to know something that it is difficult for your conscious mind to know. It may be about your sexuality, a grief, trauma, your family, betrayal, shame, vocation, a relationship, fears about illness, spirituality, an addiction, your identity, or a moral issue.
What you don’t want to do is bully your subconscious with statements like,
“Why don’t you just tell me?” “What are you hiding?” “Tell me right now!” or “I demand that you reveal the truth!”

This can lead to flooding, panic, false certainty, confabulation, dissociation, and just generally making your day suck more. When you’re flooded, it can be hard to access your adult capacities to pause, choose, reality test, plan and make choices for yourself. Until your adult has enough of these capacities, especially regulation and support, it is not good for your subconscious to communicate with you. Silence is safer. But when your adult does have enough regulation, support, humility, and other capacities, you can talk with your subconscious.

“What do you need for my conscious mind to be able to know what you’re saying 5% better?” “Can you tell me through a symbol?” “Can you tell me what you need me to do to be safe without telling me what it is?” “Do you need me to get support to be able to know what it is? Who?”

You may even want to say, “Dear wise subconscious mind, if there is something you know that my conscious mind can’t handle, please don’t just break it open in a way that isn’t good for me. Please prepare me to hear it in a way that is safe. Ground me. Get me support. Tell me what to do.”
REMEMBER: Hypnotic imagery is not always literal, especially around trauma and memory.

old: Do not treat inner voices, images, autonomous movements, or body signals as commands or proof. Listen, then reality-test.
new: DO NOT: See the voices, images, movements or body signals as real, but always reality test them.

old: Do not chase grand downloads or turn demons, jinn, and “Unattached Burdens” into a hobby. Stabilize first, and seek help when reality-testing or function weakens.
new: DO NOT obsess about “downloading” grandiose information or become obsessed with demons, jinn, “Unattached Burdens”, etc. Stabilize yourself. Get help if necessary, especially if not reality testing well or if not functioning well in life.

old: Do not use self-hypnosis while driving, bathing, swimming, operating equipment, supervising children, or doing anything that requires active attention.
new: DO NOT do self-hypnosis while driving a car, bathing, swimming, or otherwise doing something that requires active participation.

old: Do not force memory recovery, use trance to prove what happened, or suppress medical symptoms.
new: DO NOT try to “force” memories to “prove” something to yourself or ignore medical symptoms by “forcing” them down through hypnosis.

old: Do not override hunger, fatigue, pain, grief, anger, or fear before understanding the signal.
new: DO NOT “force” yourself to ignore basic body signals, like hunger, tiredness, pain, etc., or basic emotions, like grief, anger, fear, etc.

old: Do not prolong altered states indefinitely or treat intuition as fact without testing it.
new: DO NOT “extend” altered states indefinitely or take intuitive hits as “real” without reality testing them.

old: Keep the inner roles in proportion: the child does not lead adult life; the Protector cannot exclude all love; the Nurturer cannot erase consequences; the Leader cannot bypass the child; analysis and tenderness both remain available.
new: DO NOT allow any inner state, like the “Inner Child” or “Protector” or “Nurturer” or “Leader” to take over completely. They each need the others.

old: Do not use NLP to override protectors, manufacture certainty, manipulate anyone, or perform healing when the body says no.
new: DO NOT use NLP techniques to “force” down “protectors” or to do anything else that does not make logical sense, like to manipulate people or to “heal” something that the body is saying cannot be healed.

old: Doubt, distraction, resistance, silence, and “no” do not prove that an induction is working.
new: Don’t convince yourself that negative indicators like doubt, distraction, resistance, or lack of response, or saying “No” are good indicators that the induction is working.

old: “The unconscious will keep me safe” does not replace clear limits, a safe setting, the ability to stop, and a tested exit.
new: Don’t rely solely upon the “safety” of “the unconscious mind”. Always make certain that the circumstances are as safe as possible and that there is a safe way out.

old: Ordinary sensations do not prove hidden trauma, illness, toxicity, possession, attachment, transformation, or subconscious truth.
new: Don’t believe that normal physical sensations are indicators of trauma, illness, body toxins, demonic possession, “attachments”, “transformations” or anything else, just because the “subconscious” says they are.

old: Imagined repair does not establish physical recovery, neurological repair, cellular change, or a cure.
new: Don’t believe that anything is “healed” physically or neurologically/cellularly, simply because it is “healed” in the imagination.

old: Do not install hidden instructions, undisclosed third-party activation, compulsory behavior, identity switching, or amnesia. A consciously chosen reusable cue should have a clear purpose, remain reviewable, and be retired if it becomes unwanted; saying “cancel” does not guarantee instant erasure.
new: Don’t ever allow anyone to put “commands” in without giving them to yourself consciously and knowing why and wanting them, so that they can be used repeatedly and reviewed and removed if they are no longer wanted. There is no way to “put something in” that cannot be removed, but saying “I remove them” may not be enough. Don’t allow anyone to give commands to someone else to give to “YOU” or to make YOU do anything or change to a different person or have amnesia, etc.

old: End every waking session with ordinary identity, movement, orientation, judgment, and a direct statement that the session has ended.
new: DO bring yourself back to normal consciousness as yourself at the end of each session while awake.

old: Use self-hypnosis as a relationship with yourself. When the situation needs actual care, the guide shouldn’t become a substitute for it.
new: Self-hypnosis is a relationship you have with yourself, and sometimes the situation calls for more than that.

old: Get urgent help now for immediate danger, severe confusion, inability to keep yourself safe, or concerning physical symptoms such as chest pain or fainting. New or worsening suicidal thoughts, severe insomnia, mania-like or psychosis-like symptoms, or dissociation that disrupts functioning need prompt professional assessment, not a four-to-twelve-week practice schedule.
new: Get urgent help now if you’re confused, in danger, or experiencing physical symptoms like chest pain or fainting. If you’re experiencing new or worsening suicidal thoughts, severe insomnia, or symptoms of mania or psychosis, or if your dissociative symptoms are impacting your functioning, please get help for those promptly, rather than trying to fix them with this 4- to 12-week practice.

old: For ordinary learning, start with shorter sessions, warmth, a manageable subject, and a full return. Over a week or two, track one target—anxiety, daydreaming, relationship repair, an avoided task, sleep, emotional regulation, or intuitive accuracy. Worsening function or growing certainty about unverifiable memories calls for reassessment, not more intensity.
new: On the other hand, you may need very little more support. Start small—do shorter practices, make them warm, choose a small and tractable subject to work with, make sure you’re coming all the way back out of hypnosis, and track the effect on one target area (anxiety, chronic daydreaming, repairing a relationship, getting something done, sleep, emotional regulation, intuitive accuracy, etc.) for a week or two. If you find that your functioning worsens or you’re gaining certainty about something that can’t be verified, then it may be time to reassess.

old: Seek suitable ongoing help for recurring panic, compulsive behavior, substance-related destabilization, or major relationship instability.
new: Get some other appropriate help if you’re dealing with recurring panic attacks, compulsive behaviors, substance-related destabilization, or major relationship instability.

old: Use a trauma-informed clinician trained in the method, present with you, for deliberate trauma-focused regression, searching for unknown traumatic origins through an affect or somatic bridge, or work with substantial flashbacks or dissociative reactions. A bridge follows associations from a feeling or sensation; regression revisits recalled or imagined younger experience. Either can have different uses, including resourcing. Ask what is intended and how uncertainty and unexpected reactions will be handled. Hypnosis cannot prove a historical event, even with a clinician present.
new: If you want to deliberately use regression to explore the origins of a traumatic experience that you don’t know, to follow an affect or somatic bridge to unknown traumatic origins, or if you expect substantial flashback or dissociative reactions, work with a trauma-informed trained clinician who is trained in the method you’re using and who is present while you do it. (Affect and somatic bridges mean following associations from an emotional or bodily feeling; regression means remembering or imagining what it would have been like when you were younger. Both can also be used for more stable purposes, like finding resources.) Even if you work with a clinician, please note that hypnosis can’t prove what did or didn’t happen in your life.

old: Trauma history, tears, or wanted difficult feelings don’t automatically exclude self-practice. Choose the working range with attention to the actual response and available support. Some people need a narrow range; others much broader. Confidence alone doesn’t supply missing support.
new: Having a history of trauma, crying when you access inner children, or even wanting to feel difficult feelings, doesn’t necessarily mean you need more support than working on your own. It is up to you to find how wide or narrow a range to work in, and that will be different for different people.

old: Major trauma guidelines emphasize treatments such as trauma-focused CBT variants, CPT, PE, and EMDR depending on the person and guideline. Self-hypnosis and inner-child practice may support that process, but high-risk trauma work needs a larger container.
new: Most guidelines for treating major trauma recommend some variant of trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy, such as cognitive processing therapy, prolonged exposure, or eye movement desensitization and reprocessing. Self-hypnosis and inner child work can be part of that process. If you’re working with high-risk trauma, you may want a bigger container for that work.

old: If the practice makes ordinary life more loving, honest, functional, relational, grounded, and precise, continue gently. If it makes ordinary life less stable, stop deepening and return to sleep, food, grounding, boundaries, and outside support.
new: The ultimate feedback on whether your process is working well is how you’re functioning in ordinary life. If you’re being more loving, honest, functional, relational, grounded, and precise than you were before you started, then keep doing what you’re doing. If you’re functioning less well than before, then stop trying to go deeper and focus instead on getting enough sleep, eating, grounding yourself, maintaining healthy boundaries with others, and getting support from others.

old: The subconscious isn’t the enemy. Neither are the body, the sharp analytical mind, or the protector that has been braced for years. Most of them have been trying to help without ever being properly introduced.
new: Most of these things will become easier once you stop being afraid of your subconscious and your body, and when you stop fighting your analytical mind or whatever protector is up at the time.

old: I’m less interested in how deeply you can get hypnotized than whether you become an adult you can trust.
new: Also, I’m far more concerned about you becoming a trustworthy adult than about how deep you can go into hypnosis.

old: Listen until the kid is willing to come closer. Keep enough small promises that the guards can occasionally sit down. Love yourself enough that thought stops bracing against tenderness, and think clearly enough that love doesn’t drift into fantasy. Then take the practice back into ordinary life, where the adult keeps the promise.
new: Then listen to her when she wants to come closer. It’s easiest if you keep some of your promises to her, too, because then the guards can relax a bit. Work on loving yourself, so that your thought processes don’t fight it, and work on thinking about yourself, so that your love doesn’t slip off into fantasy. Work on applying this to your regular life, too, so that your adult can keep the promise.

old: Use the Inner Signal app to get voice hypnosis sessions, learn the method, develop your own language, reflect on what you report, and ask questions about a hypnotist’s approach. Self-hypnosis doesn’t require an app, and finding a practitioner is an option rather than a graduation requirement.
new: Welcome to Inner Signal, the app designed to help you take your first steps into the world of hypnosis. Here you’ll find several voice-recorded sessions to guide you, information about the method you’re using, and tips on how to develop your own language for hypnotic self-talk. After each session, you’ll have the chance to report what went through your mind and body, and consider what you might have missed, so you can learn to catch more of your inner experience next time. You can also ask the app questions about how a hypnotherapist might approach particular issues. You don’t need an app to do self-hypnosis, and you don’t have to graduate from this app before looking for a practitioner to work with, but it may help to have a starting point.

old: In the ChatGPT version, an uploaded picture or drawing, a poem, or a song can be the starting point rather than a prose explanation. Use material the current chat can actually inspect; it should say when it cannot open an image or hear audio. What the material contains, what it means to you, and the app’s interpretation are different things. You can correct the interpretation without having to justify your choice of expression.
new: If you’re using the ChatGPT version of this app, you might want to upload a picture, drawing, poem or song to talk about instead of writing out your explanation in prose. But please make sure the file you upload can be seen or heard by the chat you’re currently using! It will probably tell you that it can’t see or hear the file if you’ve made this mistake. Please remember that what you say about what’s in the file, what it means to you, and what the app thinks it means, are three different things, and that you get to decide for yourself whether the app has interpreted it correctly – you don’t have to defend your choice of medium.

old: Keep in mind that even with voice, an app has to ask what is happening. It cannot feel your body, share a practitioner’s embodied intuition, or know an unreported response. Its role is to help you learn and make better-informed choices, not pretend to be a skilled therapist.

out: Appendix C: The extended de-hypnosis checklist
Use this list for any person, ad, ideology, spiritual teaching, romantic attraction, or voice in your head…
If you can’t stand the test… there’s something you don’t want you to notice.
Questions to ask yourself before acting on anything…
Is there any sense of urgency in the delivery?
Is there any sense of secrecy in the delivery?
Is there any shame or fear in the delivery?
Does it tell you that you’re wrong or bad or not enough and only they/it can help you fix it?
Does it tell you that you’re special or chosen and only they/it understands you?
Is there any sense of sexual charge in the delivery?
Is there a sense of spiritual superiority in the delivery?
Does it want anything from you (money, sex, loyalty, silence, etc)?
Does it pressure you for anything and make you feel like you don’t have other choices?
Is your questioning or the questioning of others described as resistance?
Is your resistance to something described as a problem that needs to be overcome?
Is the delivery down-grading ordinary life or your ability to succeed in it on your own?
Is the delivery targeting your child self (enticing, scaring, rescuing, etc)?
Does it let your adult self make the final decision?

If you answer yes to several of these questions, it’s time to slow down, not go deeper into trance, and re-gain contact with your body, your food, your rest, your time, and others who can help you figure out what’s going on.

A good guide will increase your adult self. A bad guide will replace your adult self with something else. A good guide will respect your “no.” A bad guide will describe your “no” as resistance, ego, fear, low vibrational energy, past life or childhood trauma, sin, etc, and say that what you need is more of their guidance to help you get over your “no.”
For hypnosis specifically, you might want to add:
Are the induction mechanics openly communicated to you ahead of time?
Is there at least one way to answer each question that will bring you to full alertness, cause the hypnosis to be modified, or cause the hypnosis to be stopped entirely?
Does the delivery indicate that not noticing is a good thing and something you shouldn’t tell anyone else?
Does the induction use concepts like role, ownership, obedience, age, identity, belonging, etc, to get you to step out of your adult self?
Are the effects of fractionation, cues, etc, on your later behavior and memory openly communicated to you ahead of time?
Does the induction try to make you doubt or discount your body’s experience by imposing concepts on it?
Does the exit restore you to full use of your ordinary identity and critical faculties and let you know that the session is over?
If you can’t answer yes to all of these, bring yourself to full alertness and ask to see the script or for the hypnosis to be modified.

out: Appendix D: Anxiety — body first

Anxiety is usually a Protector trying to prevent something bad from happening, such as danger, shame, abandonment, failure, exposure, illness, rejection, loss of control, or anything else it believes would be intolerable. Don't cross-examine it! Instead, start with:
Body, Inner child, Inquiry, Action.
Inner child love:
Try the hand on heart and hand on solar plexus technique :
Little one, it's ok, you don't have to solve this, you don't have to do anything. I am here. I am with you. You are loved.
Make sure you say this with all your love for the little one, not as some incantation you hope will trick your subconscious into shutting up.
Reduced breathing:
If you tend to overbreathe and panic, you may want to try the Buteyko method of reduced breathing . Be aware that increased air hunger can increase anxiety at first, so go slow:

Inhale a small amount through your nose, exhale quietly, and pause for a little bit before you inhale again. If this starts to make you feel panicky, dizzy, or if you have other medical reasons to suspect it's a bad idea, stop.
EFT Tapping :

This is another mostly bodily technique that may be worth trying while we wait for more research. A 2025 systematic review showed that, at that time, there were seven RCTs done on EFT for anxiety disorders. Although the evidence should be taken with a grain of salt compared to first-line therapies, EFT helped more than no intervention in several trials.
Even though I am afraid of X, I am still willing to love myself.
Somatic Experiencing:
More info and a free intro session to my Somatic Guide here:
Where is the activation? Where is neutral? Can you move slowly back and forth between the two places?
Gendlin Focusing:
What is your felt sense of the anxiety as a whole?
Again, don't try to answer this from your head. Get a vague overall felt sense of the whole thing in your body, and then:
What does this felt sense need me to know?

Try out some words or phrases to see if they match the felt sense. Then investigate the situation. Just because something matches the felt sense doesn't mean it's correct, but it's a place to start. And if your words don't match your felt sense, you can reexamine your words.

Other things you can try with your body when your mind is too activated for meditation to help: massage your foot, scalp, temple, neck (not the front!), or shoulders; apply warmth or pressure; use a weighted blanket; turn off the lights; put on music that usually calms you down; or use a massage gun (avoid injured, numb, bruised, inflamed, or recently surgically operated areas, as well as varicose veins, and stop if you feel pain, dizziness, tingling, or other bad symptoms).

Different people respond to different things, so find what works for you: lights off, warmth, music, massage, weighted blanket, breathwork, comforting object, or your favorite piece of relaxation technology (ozonated charcoal "holy water" and Blushield are two of my favorites; more info on my ZHoly3O page).
Finally, here's a script to talk yourself through anxiety:
I'll start with my body.
Little one, it's ok, I'm here. Protector, it's ok, I hear you, thank you for looking out for me.
If there's something I need to do, I'll do it. If there's nothing to do, I'll stand my body down.
Either way, I won't abandon you or worship you, I'll just listen, reality check, and do what's needed.

old: Daydreaming can be intuition, simulation, grief digestion, creative rehearsal, symbolic teaching, or the subconscious showing a possible future, fear, or desire. It can also become avoidance, fantasy addiction, dissociation, romantic obsession, or an escape hatch from adult life.
Does the daydream return me to life with more clarity, love, and action? Or does it pull me away from life into repetition, craving, and avoidance?
When it seems useful, ask:
“What is the guidance inside this?”
When it seems to be pulling you away, change the body before debating the story. Sit upright. Open the eyes a little. Feel the feet.

“Subconscious, thank you for showing me images. If this daydream is useful, please reveal the guidance inside it. If it is avoidance, please bring me gently into the present and help me deal with what I need to deal with in a gentle but structured way.”
Then get embarrassingly practical:
“What real-life action is this daydream replacing?”

The answer may be: send the message, stop sending the message, clean the room, eat, sleep, grieve, create, apologize, leave, tell the truth, make the plan, ask for help, return to the task, or stop chasing unavailable love.
new: Sometimes, daydreaming is intuitive. Your subconscious is simulating an idea or event to help you digest trauma or teach you something. The act of daydreaming may also be a creative exercise or a way your subconscious is telling you about the future. Sometimes your subconscious will show you things you’re afraid of, so you can learn to deal with them. Sometimes it shows you what you want.

Other times, it’s a detriment. An escape from reality. An addiction to fantasy rather than reality. Dissociation from the pain of real life. Obsession with romantic partners. Refusal to accept the responsibilities of adult life.
How do you know which one it is? Ask yourself, “Is my daydreaming bringing me back into life or taking me away from it?”
If it’s helping you, ask for more specific guidance.

If it’s taking you away from life, immediately sit up straight and open your eyes. Then ask your subconscious for help. “Hey subconscious, thanks for all these interesting images. If they’re helpful, please show me what I need to know. If they’re just a way for me to avoid dealing with life, please bring me into the present and show me how to deal with life in a gentle but structured way.”
Then ask yourself, “What do I need to do in the real world that I’m avoiding by daydreaming?”

It could be anything from “send a text message” or “stop sending text messages” to “clean my room” or “eat” or “sleep” or “deal with my grief” or “create something” or “apologize” or “leave someone” or “tell the truth” or “make a plan” or “get help” or “return to the task at hand” or “stop fantasizing about people who can’t love me.”

old: This guide doesn’t tell anyone to use substances. It does acknowledge that many people first encounter self-hypnosis, inner-child contact, or Higher Self dialogue while altered.
Do not use altered states to force revelation. Use them to deepen listening, strengthen love, and improve ordinary life.

A past opening can be a resource without becoming a state you must reproduce. Having experienced love once, being able to access it only in a particular state, and contacting it reliably in daily life are different things. Let the experience widen what seems possible while you build usable access. If the child cannot receive it, meet the difficulty rather than escalating the intensity.
During or after an altered state, these prompts are usually more useful than demanding a revelation:
“Help me stay grounded.” “Help me receive only what I can integrate.” “Help me remember love.” “Help me return when it is time.” “Help me translate this into one ordinary-life change.”
Don’t use self-hypnosis to prolong an altered state indefinitely, recover memories, intensify fear, bypass sleep, override medical needs, or make yourself less able to communicate.
If the state makes you less loving, less grounded, less honest, less able to sleep, less able to communicate, or less able to meet ordinary responsibilities, stop deepening and start integrating.
new: Mind Altered States & Inner Child Work Note: I am NOT encouraging anyone to use these. However, many people do attempt their first self-hypnosis, contact with their inner child or contact with their Higher Self while in a mind altered state.
If you choose to do so, please be aware that you should not use this state to force open anything, but rather use it to enhance your ability to love and improve your life.

Many people have opened to certain things in their life in altered states. The key is that though it is great that this opened, it is different to have had the experience of love, to be able to access it in a particular state and to be able to access it on a day to day basis. Sometimes if the child can't take it, you may need to open the experience up a bit more.

So if you are in an altered state, rather than asking for a revelation, you may want to use these phrases: Help me to ground. Help me to only take that which I can integrate. Help me to remember the love I am feeling. Help me to come back again when the time is right. Help me to take something from this and change my regular life.

You should not use self-hypnosis to keep you in an altered state forever, to help you remember things, to make you more afraid, to help you not sleep, to not see a doctor, or to not communicate with other people.

If you find that being in an altered state is helping you to love less, to be more ungrounded, to be less honest, to not sleep, to not communicate or to not do regular life things, then you should stop attempting to go deeper and instead work on integrating what you have.

old: Self-hypnosis can become very powerful during loveyhuasca, meditation, lucid dreaming, grief, sexual energy, prayer, sleep loss, or other plant-medicine-adjacent states. Sometimes the mind opens faster than the adult self can organize what is arriving.

Intensity then gets mistaken for meaning. Sometimes the inner child is finally speaking. Sometimes a Protector is showing fear, or shame, grief, anger, longing, and other buried material are asking for care. But an intense state can also be bodily overload, environmental chaos, sleep deprivation, or plain confusion. A frightening image isn’t automatically truth, a bad feeling isn’t automatically a lesson, and a “download” doesn’t deserve belief merely because it came with excellent lighting.
Before trying to interpret the state, ask a simpler question:
“What kind of problem is happening?”
new: Self-hypnosis can be extremely powerful when used in altered states of consciousness such as when one is loveyhuasca, meditating, in a lucid dream, grieving, utilizing sexual energy, praying, not sleeping, or in other states similar to plant medicines.

The problem is that people think that because they are in an altered state, that it must mean something. Sometimes it is your inner child talking, sometimes it is a Protector scaring you, and sometimes it is shame/grief/anger or other parts coming out, but often it is simply your body being overloaded by the experience, the chaos of the environment, lack of sleep, or some other reason that it just doesn't make sense. Just because you had a picture that scared you doesn't mean it's true, just because you had a bad feeling doesn't mean it's helpful and just because you had a download in a nice lighting doesn't mean you should believe it.
Before trying to interpret what is happening in an altered state, you should
“What kind of problem is happening?”
